title: Construction Permit Automation: From Application to Inspection
summary: How permit coordinators automate city and county portal work with Skyvern: applications, uploads, status checks and inspection requests, no code.
body_markdown:
If your team is managing permits across several jurisdictions, coordinators have to work through different forms and document requirements. They re-enter project details and upload files, then return to each portal to check progress. Correction notices bring another round of revised documents and follow-up. Each new project adds more records and inspection requests for the same team to track.


We built Skyvern to take that repetitive browser work off people’s hands so teams can manage more projects. An agent can work through permit portals and return results for your team to review.


In this article, we show you how to use Skyvern to prepare permit applications, monitor their progress, and manage inspection requests. We explain where to include human review and how to test a workflow on one portal before expanding to other jurisdictions.


## What is construction permit automation?


Construction permit automation uses software to perform repeatable tasks involved in preparing, submitting, and managing permit applications. That can include entering project details, uploading documents, collecting application numbers, checking status, downloading issued permits, and requesting inspections.


Applicant-side automation helps contractors, developers, and permit coordinators handle more projects through existing city and county systems in the United States. It reduces the repetitive portal work your team needs to do for each application.


Skyvern handles browser interactions within the process. Your project team supplies the project facts and approved documents, while the permitting authority determines the application's outcome under its process.


## Government permitting systems vs applicant-side automation


Cities automate their side of permitting with the systems they buy, and applicants still have to work through those portals. That applicant-side portal work is the part Skyvern automates. When you search for permit automation, you find three kinds of tools, built for different people:


- **Government permitting platforms** are what a city or county buys to receive, review, and issue permits. OpenGov says its Permitting & Licensing product "helps state and local governments process building permits, licenses, inspections, and code enforcement." Accela, Trimble Unity Permit, and Salesforce also sell permitting software to public agencies.
- **Applicant-side permit software** handles permits for builders. PermitFlow uses agents to submit applications and track updates from jurisdictions. Pulley provides permitting services supported by AI.
- **Browser automation** lets your own team keep the permit work in-house and automate the portal steps it repeats. With Skyvern, the coordinators who already file the permits build the workflows themselves, so the team can manage permits for more projects without hiring more people.


Permit expediters and some permit software providers offer services to handle applications on your behalf. Checking a design against the building code before you apply is a separate job, and it happens before any of this portal work.


## Why permit work is still so manual


Permit applications are still very manual because the information is scattered, requirements vary, and the work continues after submission.


### Project information lives in different places


The project address might be in your project management system, contractor details in a spreadsheet, and drawings in a shared folder. Someone has to gather that information, check that it's current, and enter it into the permit portal. Across multiple applications, your team ends up repeatedly moving information it already has.


### Jurisdictions have different requirements


A process that works for one city may need adjustments for the next. Permit categories, required fields, supporting documents, and submission steps can differ. Your team has to check each jurisdiction’s requirements and work through its process, even when the projects themselves are similar. A single project might also need several permits, such as building, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and grading, each with its own application.


### Documents need preparation


Having the drawings ready doesn't mean the submission package is ready. Someone still has to select the correct versions, follow file-naming rules, and upload documents into the required folders or categories. If the portal rejects a file, your team has to identify the problem, fix it, and confirm the replacement uploaded successfully.


### Applications need follow-up


Submitting the application doesn't finish the work. Someone has to check its status, retrieve review comments, and get each request to the person who can resolve it. When revised documents are ready, your team has to upload them and respond to the outstanding comments. Each correction cycle adds another round of coordination.


## Which parts of the permit process can you automate?


Automate the applicant's admin: data entry, uploads, and status checks. Leave design answers and the city's review to people.


The time spent on a permit comes from three kinds of work:


- Applicant administration, such as entering data, uploading files, and checking status.
- Project work, such as answering a technical question or revising a drawing.
- The authority's review and approval process.


Skyvern can take on repetitive browser actions in the first category and help move information between the others. The time saved by your coordinator is measurable even when the authority's review timeline stays the same.


Start with a task you can describe clearly, including what the agent should return. These are workflow patterns to configure and test against your actual portals.


Task Inputs to provide Work to automate Result to check


Prepare an application Approved project information and selected permit type Enter fields and navigate conditional pages Saved application and a list of unanswered questions


Upload documents Required files, versions, and document categories Select and upload each specified file Portal attachment list matches the document manifest


Submit an approved application Reviewed application and authorization to submit Complete the permitted submission steps Application reference and submission confirmation


Monitor progress Application reference and checking schedule Open the record and extract its current state Exact portal status, timestamp, and new notices


Handle correspondence Application reference and responsible team member Retrieve correction requests and supporting files Notice delivered to the person responsible for responding


Retrieve issued permits Issued record Download documents Saved permit files


Request inspections Approved inspection type and availability Request an available appointment Confirmed inspection details


## How Skyvern works across permit portals


You can reuse the overall sequence of tasks across permit portals because Skyvern works out which fields to fill and which controls to use on each page. Your team still needs to check each portal’s requirements and test the workflow.


Skyvern opens a browser, examines a screenshot and the page's structure, and uses an LLM to choose its next action. It can then interact with the page and check the resulting state. Our[architecture documentation explains that loop](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/concepts#how-skyvern-works) .


For a permit form, that means the agent can use field labels and page context to locate the address input, interact with dropdowns, and respond when a selection reveals additional questions. It reduces the amount of fixed navigation and field-location logic you need to maintain.


If a portal provides a supported API that covers the required actions, it may be the simplest integration. Browser automation helps with work that remains inside the website, particularly when you need to navigate several different systems.


Reuse the project-data model and the workflow pattern across jurisdictions, then validate each portal's requirements and behavior.


## How to build the first permit workflow in Skyvern


This walkthrough assumes your portal supports saved drafts and your team has checked the project information and documents. The workflow treats application preparation, approved submission, and ongoing monitoring as three connected pieces so you can test each outcome separately. The diagram shows how those pieces fit together.


The steps below begin with gathering the inputs and configuring the agent.


### 1. Gather the project record and document checklist


Before opening the workflow builder, collect:


- The portal URL and the jurisdiction's current application checklist.
- Your internal project reference, site address, and parcel information where required.
- The selected permit type, approved scope description, and requested project values.
- Applicant, owner, contractor, and design-professional details where required.
- A document manifest listing each file, its version, and its destination category.
- The person responsible for reviewing the prepared application.


Keep the manifest specific. "Upload the plans" leaves room for the wrong revision. "Upload this approved drawing set to the Plans category" gives the workflow a checkable instruction.


Note each city's document rules in the manifest as well. Some jurisdictions ask for wet-stamped drawings and others accept digital signatures, so the same project can need a different file for each portal.


If your team already follows a written permit procedure, use it as the starting point. We built[SOP Upload](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/launch-week-day-4-sop-upload-to-build-new-workflows/) to turn process instructions into a workflow you can inspect and refine. Check those instructions against the current portal before running them. If there's no written procedure,[Copilot](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/cloud/studio#build-with-copilot) can build the workflow from a plain-English description, or from a recording of your coordinator doing the task once.


### 2. Create the agent and configure its inputs


Use Skyvern's[visual agent editor](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/cloud/studio) to assemble the workflow. Add input parameters for the portal, project data, and document manifest so you can supply a new project without rewriting the instructions.


Skyvern's[agent parameters](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/cloud/studio#inputs) support values including text, JSON, and file URLs. Provide files through a location the run can access, and check that access before attempting an upload.


Configure the portal login through Skyvern's credential management and reference it in the Login block. Keep passwords out of the application instructions. The[credential documentation](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/credentials#store-a-credential) covers the available storage and integration options.


Set up two-factor authentication using a configured TOTP secret for authenticator codes or a route that supplies email or SMS codes to the run. Our[2FA documentation](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/credentials#two-factor-authentication) explains those options. Test login on its own before adding the application steps.


Authenticator (TOTP) codes need the Pro or Enterprise plan, while email codes work on any plan ([pricing](https://www.skyvern.com/pricing) ). On Pro, Skyvern phone numbers for SMS codes cost $10/month per number. For Enterprise, check your agreement for phone-number pricing. Our guide to[authentication automation platforms](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/authentication-automation-platforms-enterprise/) compares the login methods portals use, and[how Skyvern handles authentication](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/how-skyvern-handles-authentication/) covers how the login is stored.


### 3. Prepare the application and verify the draft


Add a Browser Task to work through the application. Give it a defined stopping point. For this first workflow, that point is a saved draft ready for review.


An example instruction, using the parameters you created:


> Open {{ portal_url }} and prepare the permit application using {{ project_data }} and the files in {{ document_manifest }}.
>
>
> Check for an existing draft using the supplied project reference. If the matching draft is unambiguous, continue it. If multiple records match, stop and report them.
>
>
> Use only the supplied project values and documents. If a required answer is missing or a choice is ambiguous, report the question. Do not guess an answer, submit the application, pay a fee, or complete a certification.
>
>
> Save the draft where the portal allows it. Return the draft reference, current page URL, attached filenames, unresolved questions, and any validation messages shown by the portal.


Watch the first run to confirm that the agent selects the intended record, maps the inputs correctly, and uploads the specified files. Test whether it follows the prompt’s instructions before using the workflow unattended.


After the task, use extraction and validation steps to compare the saved address, applicant details, and attachment list with your inputs. A visible filename alone may not confirm that an upload finished, so check the portal’s upload status too.


### 4. Review the application before triggering submission


Have the coordinator inspect the saved draft and resolve outstanding questions. The review should cover the information entered, file versions, declarations, and any fees requiring authorization.


For this design, the preparation agent ends at the saved draft. Once review is complete, the reviewer can trigger a separate submission workflow using that draft's reference and the approved information. Recheck the current application before submitting, especially if someone has edited it since review.


On our Enterprise plan, Skyvern also offers a[Human Interaction block](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/reference/blocks) for review within a workflow. The run pauses until the reviewer approves or rejects it, and the block times out after 120 minutes by default if nobody responds, so set a timeout your reviewers can meet. For a first implementation, keep preparation and submission separate so the reviewer can control when the application is sent.


### 5. Capture what happened


Make the submission task return the portal's confirmation, and keep these details alongside the project record so your team can find the application, check its status, and follow up on outstanding work:


- Internal project reference and portal application number.
- Exact portal status and confirmation text.
- Submission or checking timestamp.
- Receipt or confirmation document, when available.
- Outstanding items and the person responsible for the next action.


A completed automation run and an approved permit are separate facts. Store both the run outcome and the permit's state.


If the portal times out after submission, inspect the application record before trying again. The submission may have succeeded even though the browser didn't receive the confirmation.


Download records you need to retain into your project repository. Skyvern's[file results can include expiring download URLs](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/developers/browser-automation#download-and-upload-files) , so a temporary link shouldn't be your only copy of a receipt or issued permit.


### 6. Add monitoring and connect the results to your team


Create a separate agent that opens the application, reads its status, and retrieves new notices. It should check existing records without starting new applications.


You can[schedule the agent in Skyvern](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/cloud/runs#schedule-an-agent) . Choose a frequency that fits the project's deadlines and the portal's usage requirements, then verify the schedule's timezone.


Your tracking system should compare each result with the previous one. Notify the responsible person when there's a meaningful change, and record failed checks so an old status doesn't look current.


If you file on several city and county portals, keep one status report across all of them, with one row per application: the jurisdiction, the exact portal status, when it was last checked, and when the status last changed. Keeping "last checked" apart from "last changed" shows you which applications are stuck and which ones nobody has looked at recently.


Use[webhooks](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/developers/production#webhooks) to receive the results when a run finishes, then configure your integration to update the project record. The scheduled portal visit discovers the change. The webhook delivers the run's result.


If your team uses Procore, Buildertrend, or another construction system, check its integration options and map the returned fields into the appropriate record. That connection is part of the implementation.


## After approval: inspection scheduling, results, and failed inspections


After a permit is issued, your team still needs to arrange inspections and follow up on the results. The monitoring agent from step 6 detects when the permit is issued, so the workflow can then request inspections, collect results, and start follow-up if an inspection fails. Each step should return a result your coordinator can check.


1. **Request the inspection.** Give the agent the permit number, the approved inspection type, and the dates the site will be ready, and have it request an available slot inside that window and return the confirmation. If no slot fits, have it report the slots it found instead of booking outside the window.
2. **Save the confirmation.** Store the inspection date, type, and confirmation number with the project record, next to the submission fields from step 5.
3. **Collect the result.** After the inspection date, have the monitoring agent read the result from the portal and download any inspection report or correction notice.
4. **Handle a failed inspection.** Route the correction notice to the trade or superintendent responsible for the fix. Once they confirm the fix, have the agent request a re-inspection.
5. **Download the final sign-off.** After all required inspections pass, save the final approval documents to your project repository when they become available.


The webhook from step 6 carries these results into your project system. An approved permit can update the project schedule, and a failed inspection can alert the superintendent without anyone checking the portal.


Some jurisdictions book inspections only by phone. Those requests stay with your team, although the agent can still read the results once the portal posts them.


## How to handle the cases that need a human decision


You want a permit workflow to make issues and unresolved work visible. A missing answer should become an assigned question, with enough context for someone to resolve it.


Design the response to common exceptions before expanding the workflow:


Situation Response to build into the process


A required answer is missing Return the field label and project reference to the owner of that information.


The portal offers several plausible permit types Ask the permit coordinator to confirm the selection.


A file is rejected or its version is unclear Preserve the error and ask for the correct document.


Login expires Reauthenticate through the configured flow, then verify the current application state.


Submission or payment has an uncertain outcome Check the portal record and receipt before repeating the action.


A correction notice requires a design change Retrieve the notice and route it to the responsible project professional.


No inspection slot fits the requested window Report the available slots and ask the superintendent to pick one or change the window.


An inspection fails Retrieve the result and correction notes, route them to the responsible trade, and request a re-inspection once the fix is confirmed.


Returning to an application also requires deliberate[session management](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/browser-automation-session-management/) . Reusing browser state can reduce repeated login work, but the portal can still expire a session or require another verification step.


Skyvern Cloud supports automatic CAPTCHA solving, although success isn't guaranteed. The solver is Basic on Hobby, Advanced on Pro, and Elite on Enterprise. Our[CAPTCHA documentation](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/developers/production#anti-bot-and-captcha) also describes manual intervention and the different behavior of self-hosted deployments. Check the deployment you intend to use.


For transient failures, use a bounded retry policy and preserve the failure reason. Our[guide to error handling in browser automation](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/error-handling-in-browser-automation/) covers that foundation. For permit workflows, add the application-specific checks above, particularly around actions that create a record or charge a fee.


## How to measure a pilot and expand it


Use a pilot to check whether the workflow saves staff time and produces reliable results before expanding it.


1. **Choose a small pilot.** Start with one permit type on a portal your coordinator knows. If application preparation involves too many unresolved decisions, begin with status checks on existing applications.
2. **Compare staff time before and during the pilot.** Measure the same work in both cases, including finding documents, entering information, reviewing results, and handling mistakes.
3. **Track reliability and costs.** Record the proportion of runs with verified outputs, how often people intervene, and the cost of running and maintaining the workflow. For monitoring, distinguish the last successful check from the last attempted check.
4. **Calculate the time saved.** A measured reduction of 20 minutes per application frees 20 hours across 60 applications. Include the time still spent on review and exceptions when calculating the reduction.
5. **Measure municipal review time separately.** Only attribute faster permit approval to automation if the pilot provides evidence for that connection.
6. **Expand when results are consistently verifiable.** Reuse the project-data model and workflow across locations. Before each new jurisdiction’s first live application, check its form requirements, document rules, login flow, and status meanings, then adjust and test the workflow.


## Try Skyvern on one permit workflow


Each stage should leave a usable record and a clear owner for unresolved work. Keep submission confirmations with project records, route correction notices to the responsible person, and retain inspection results through to final sign-off.


To try this with Skyvern, bring one portal, a sample project record, and the checklist your coordinator already uses.[Start building an agent](https://app.skyvern.com/?ref=skyvern.com) for a defined task, such as preparing a saved draft or checking an existing application’s status. Use the pilot to measure staff time and check the results, including any work that still needs human attention. Once the workflow produces results your coordinator trusts, extend it to other permit tasks and test it separately for each new jurisdiction.


## FAQ


### What happens when a portal changes its layout?


Re-test the workflow on the changed pages before its next live run. Skyvern identifies fields from the page it reads during each run. A redesign can also change the questions, required documents, or status names, so someone who knows the permit should check those.


### Can the agent handle conditional fields?


Yes. When a selection reveals new questions, the agent can read them and answer using the project data you supplied. The step 3 prompt instructs it to report questions it can't answer from that data. Test this behavior on your portal before running the workflow unattended.


### What audit trail is kept?


Each Skyvern run keeps a recording, a screenshot for each step, a timeline, and its outputs ([runs documentation](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/cloud/runs) ). Store the confirmation fields from step 5 with the project record as well, so the permit's history doesn't depend on the run history alone.


### Are we allowed to automate a city portal?


Check the portal's terms of use first. Under[our terms](https://www.skyvern.com/terms) , you're responsible for having the authority to automate the sites you use Skyvern on. If the portal offers a supported API for the task, use that instead.
